How AI for the enterprise is evolving, from owning a task to owning an outcome:

1. Assistant: handles one task in seconds, like sending a follow-up email. Companies pay for it out of their software budget.

2. Agent: handles one interaction in minutes, like a customer's refund call. It takes on work people used to do, so it gets paid for out of the labor budget.

3. Long-running agent: works toward a goal for weeks or months, like getting an injured client the biggest settlement possible. Because it owns the result, the company selling it can price on the outcome it delivers.

Nathan Lambert, former post-training co-lead at the Allen Institute for AI, now launching Trillium, a nonprofit open AI lab, joins a16z's Lisha Li to discuss whether open models can really keep up with the frontier.

When he tells researchers in China that an average OpenAI researcher reportedly has five thousand H100s to work with, "their jaw just falls to the floor." In his view, Chinese labs have the talent but are mostly short on compute.

He also thinks the distillation story is overblown. Based on the research, he puts its edge at a few months, and says "there's a bit of cope" in thinking only American labs can build good models.

A lot of frontier progress outside math and code comes down to labs buying 1) data and 2) RL environments. It's a multibillion-dollar market, and some of it is sloppy enough to teach models to reward hack.

That's a big part of why Trillium exists. Nathan wants to give away the environments other people would sell, and show exactly how his team uses AI to build AI, including where the models still get stuck. His bet is that the more people can see how this works, the better prepared everyone is for what's coming.

Until recently, AI agents mostly handled short tasks, like one support call or one email. Now they can stay on a job for weeks or months.

That matters for "relay race" work that runs through a long chain of people.

Every handoff in that chain is a chance for something to fall through: a slow callback, a dropped follow-up, lost context.

Take a personal injury case. Today it moves from intake to investigation to the demand letter, with different people at each step. A single case agent can work it from the first call to settlement, chasing witnesses, records, and bills, and keeping the client and attorney updated along the way.

The same idea applies to processes like mortgages, insurance claims, and enterprise sales.

Because the agent owns the end result, the company selling it can charge on the outcome (a closed loan, a settled case, a signed deal) and move past pricing on the labor it saves (paralegal hours, call center seats).

The bond market is repricing the cost of American debt.

US 10-year Treasury yields are up about 100 basis points this year. Apollo broke the move into its parts: a higher expected path of real short rates, and a rising term premium, the extra yield investors demand to hold long bonds. Term premium climbs when the market worries about deficits and how much debt it has to absorb.

Washington runs the deficit. Bondholders set the price, and it lands on every mortgage and every loan tied to the 10-year.
